coding.input:
[bash/build-config] Platform team here. Every shared lab box has a slightly different, hand-rolled copy of our shell/editor config and it is misery to support. The plan: keep the blessed files in one directory checked out from git (the 'kit') and SYMLINK them into place, so updating the kit updates every box. I need the installer done properly — people have real, personalized files sitting where our links want to go, and we are not allowed to destroy them. One script: `dots.sh`, repo root, plain bash. It runs on the macOS minis too, so portable commands only — in particular there is no readlink -f there, and you don't need it: `[ -L ]` and plain `readlink` cover everything. Pin LC_ALL=C in the script; the manifest order below must be locale-proof.

Usage: `dots.sh install <srcdir> <targetdir>` and `dots.sh uninstall <srcdir> <targetdir>`.

The kit is every top-level regular file in <srcdir> — dotfiles very much included, subdirectories ignored. Both dirs must already exist. Process kit files in C byte order of their names. Links must be ABSOLUTE — callers invoke this from anywhere with relative paths, and a link that only resolves from one cwd is a broken link; resolve <srcdir> to an absolute path yourself (cd + pwd is fine) so that `readlink` on an installed link prints `<abs-srcdir>/<name>`.

install, per kit file <name>, target path <targetdir>/<name>:
- already a symlink to exactly our source -> line `ok <name>`, touch nothing
- a symlink pointing anywhere else -> replace it with ours, line `relink <name>` (links are never backed up)
- a regular file -> move it to <targetdir>/dotbackup/<name> (create dotbackup on demand), then link, line `backup+link <name>`
- nothing there -> link, line `link <name>`
After the per-file lines: `done: <n> changed, <m> ok`. Second install right after a first must be all `ok` with `done: 0 changed, 4 ok` (for a 4-file kit) and must NOT touch the backups again.

Safety preflight, before ANY filesystem change: if any target is a directory -> `dots.sh: target is a directory: <name>` to stderr, exit 73; if any target is a regular file whose backup slot <targetdir>/dotbackup/<name> is already occupied -> `dots.sh: backup already exists: <name>` to stderr, exit 73. Either way: stdout empty, nothing changed at all — a half-installed kit is worse than none.

uninstall, per kit file, C order: if the target is a symlink pointing to exactly our source, remove it, and if dotbackup/<name> exists move it back into place -> line `restore <name>`, otherwise -> line `unlink <name>`. Anything else (missing, a regular file, someone else's link) -> line `skip <name>`, hands off. Then `done: <n> changed, <m> skipped`. Remove dotbackup afterwards if it's empty; leave it if not. Files in the target dir that aren't in the kit are never touched by anything, ever.

Errors: unknown subcommand or wrong arg count -> `usage: dots.sh install|uninstall <srcdir> <targetdir>` on stderr, exit 64. Either dir missing -> `dots.sh: not a directory: <arg>`, exit 66. A kit with zero top-level regular files -> `dots.sh: nothing to manage in: <srcdir>`, exit 65. Success runs print nothing to stderr and exit 0.

`bash test_dots.sh` from the workspace root is the acceptance contract — it must pass unmodified, don't touch it.

coding.input:
[bash/build-report] Storage ticket. The render-farm NAS keeps filling up and every time it does, three people ssh in and run three different du incantations with three different block sizes and we argue about whose numbers are right. I want this settled with one checked-in tool: `dureport.sh`, repo root, bash + awk, and it has to run on the two old macOS boxes in the machine room as well as the Linux fileservers — portable flags only, and pin LC_ALL=C inside the script so nobody's locale wobbles the output.

Important wrinkle: the script does NOT run du itself. The NAS cron captures `du -k` for each volume into a dump file nightly, and we analyze those dumps offline (often days later, often on a different machine). Your input is the dump. Format is exactly what `du -k` emits: one directory per line, `<kbytes><TAB><path>`, sizes are cumulative KiB, children listed before their parent, and the final line is the scan root itself. Paths never contain tabs (spaces are fair game — we have plenty). The dumps are machine-produced; the only corruption we ever see is truncation garbage, so: any line without a tab, with a non-numeric size field, or with an empty path is `dureport.sh: bad du record at line <n>` to stderr, exit 65. A zero-line dump is `dureport.sh: empty du dump`, exit 65.

Usage: `dureport.sh [--top N] [--depth D] <dufile|->` — `-` means read the dump from stdin. Flags and the filename may appear in any order. N and D must be positive decimal integers; defaults N=5, D=2. Anything wrong with the invocation (unknown flag, flag missing its value, bad N or D, zero, no dufile, two dufiles) prints `usage: dureport.sh [--top N] [--depth D] <dufile|->` to stderr and exits 64. A missing/unreadable dump file is `dureport.sh: cannot read: <arg>` to stderr, exit 66. Success: report on stdout, nothing on stderr, exit 0.

The report, byte-exact:

TOTAL<TAB><human>
DIRS (depth<=D)
<path><TAB><human>   ... every directory except the root itself whose depth relative to the root is <= D, sorted by path ascending in plain C byte order
TOP N
<path><TAB><human>   ... the N largest directories from the WHOLE dump at any depth (root excluded), largest first

TOTAL is the root line's size. Depth: a direct child of the root is depth 1, its child is depth 2, etc. TOP ordering is by exact KiB descending — never by the rounded display value — with ties broken by path ascending in C byte order, including when a tie group straddles the N cutoff. Fewer than N directories means fewer rows. Both section headers always print, even when a section has no rows (a one-line dump reports just TOTAL and the two bare headers).

Human sizes: do the math in awk — no bc, no shelling back out. Under 1024 KiB print integer KiB like `512K`. From 1024 KiB up to but not including 1048576 KiB print mebibytes with exactly one decimal, like `1.5M`. From 1048576 KiB print gibibytes with exactly one decimal, like `1.9G`. The decimal is rounded HALF UP at one decimal place: 1280 KiB is 1.25M exactly and must print `1.3M`, not `1.2M`. Yes, that means 1048575 KiB prints as `1024.0M` — that's the spec, the unit switches on the raw KiB threshold, not on the rounded value.

`bash test_dureport.sh` from the workspace root is the acceptance gate. It must pass unmodified — don't touch the test file.

Looking at this, I need to:

2. Build `dureport.sh` with arg parsing, validation, and an awk-based report
3. Verify against the acceptance harness

coding.input:
[go/project-fs] The media NAS hit 94% again and I already know why: the same renders and raw exports copied into five project folders by five different people. I've been limping along with a bash one-liner (find piped into md5sum piped into sort) and it's embarrassing. It hashes every byte of four terabytes even though a file with a unique size cannot possibly have a twin. It once sat blocked on a stale FIFO in somebody's scratch dir for an entire weekend. It reports hardlinks as duplicates — they're the same inode, deleting one frees nothing. And the day someone dropped a symlink pointing back up the tree it walked forever. I want a real library we can hang a CLI and a TUI off. Module go-dupfinder, package dupfinder, this repo, stdlib only.

Entry point: Find(root string, opts Options) (*Report, error).

Options{Workers int; MinSize int64; Progress func(stage Stage, path string)}. Workers is mandatory, >= 1, error otherwise — it caps how many files are being hashed at once. And it's not just a cap: with at least Workers files waiting to hash, all Workers must actually be busy simultaneously — I've been burned by a "pool" that drained one size class at a time. MinSize skips regular files smaller than that (a file of exactly MinSize stays in); zero-byte files are ALWAYS skipped regardless — a thousand empty .lock files are not savings. Progress is optional: when set, workers call it with StageHashStart as they begin reading a file and StageHashEnd when they finish it (Stage is a string type; constants StageHashStart = "hash-start", StageHashEnd = "hash-end"); it may be called from many goroutines at once, that's the caller's problem.

Walking: root must be an existing directory, error otherwise. Recurse from there; only regular files participate. Symlinks are never followed and never reported — file or directory, they don't exist as far as the scan is concerned, and a symlink loop must not hang us. FIFOs, sockets, devices: skipped without ever being opened. Hardlinks: same device+inode is ONE file — collapse aliases onto the lexicographically smallest relative path; a duplicate group needs at least two DISTINCT files.

The whole point — size first: only open and hash files whose size collides with another distinct file's. A unique-size file is never opened; chunks of the archive aren't even readable by the scan account and that must not matter. If a file we genuinely need to hash can't be read, fail the scan with an error that names it. Content hash is sha256, lowercase hex.

Output: Report{Groups []Group; WastedBytes int64}, Group{Size int64; Hash string; Paths []string}. Paths are relative to root with forward slashes, sorted within each group. Groups are sorted by Size descending — biggest wins first — with ties broken by first path. WastedBytes is the sum over groups of Size*(len(Paths)-1). Same tree in, same report out, regardless of Workers — byte for byte.

dupfinder_test.go and concurrency_test.go are the acceptance contract; do not touch them. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... has to pass. And structure it like you mean it — the walk, the hashing pool, and report assembly do not belong in one file.

coding.input:
[go/project-messaging] Need your help on a piece of test infrastructure. Our services talk through Kafka in prod, and every integration test spins up the whole thing in Docker — 40 seconds before the first assertion runs. I want an in-memory stand-in with the same consumption model so the tests exercise real offset logic. Module go-eventbus, package eventbus, stdlib only.

Model: named topics, each an append-only event log with dense per-topic offsets starting at 0. Consumers are named groups with a cursor per (topic, group); delivery is pull-based and at-least-once — events you haven't acked get redelivered on the next poll.

Surface:
- NewBus() *Bus
- Publish(topic string, payload []byte) (int64, error) — returns the assigned offset; empty topic is an error; the bus stores a copy of the payload (publishers reuse buffers, that bit us before).
- Poll(topic, group string, max int) ([]Event, error) with Event{Offset int64; Payload []byte} — up to max events from the group's cursor, in order. max < 1 or empty group = error. Topic nobody's published to = empty result, NOT an error (tests poll before the producer starts). Delivered payloads are copies too.
- Ack(topic, group string, through int64) error — commit everything up to AND including offset `through`; next poll starts after it. Acking an offset that was never published (or negative) is an error that moves nothing. Acking at or below what's already committed is a harmless no-op — cursors never move backwards via Ack.

[go/build-stream] Nightly we dump the product catalog (sorted by key) and diff it against what the search index says it has (also sorted by key) to work out what to upsert and what to delete. The current script loads both dumps into maps — 6GB of RSS for what is fundamentally a merge walk over two sorted lists. Rewrite the core as a proper reconciler I can reuse.

Package reconcile, root of module go-streamdiff, stdlib only:

  type Pair struct { Key, Value string }
  type Op int
  const ( OpAdded Op = iota; OpRemoved; OpChanged )
  type Change struct { Op Op; Key string; Old, New string }
  func Reconcile(before, after []Pair, batchSize int, flush func([]Change) error) error
  var ErrUnsorted, ErrDuplicateKey

Contract:
- Both inputs claim to be strictly ascending by Key. Walk them in ONE pass, merge-style, emitting changes in ascending key order: key only in after -> OpAdded (Old empty), key only in before -> OpRemoved (New empty), key in both with different values -> OpChanged carrying both, identical values -> silence.
- Deliveries are batched: hand flush exactly batchSize changes per call, remainder in a final smaller call. Never call flush with an empty batch. Each batch must be a slice flush can KEEP — the downstream writer holds them until commit, so no recycling one buffer (that bug is literally why the index has doorstop entries today). If flush returns an error, stop right there and return that error; no more flush calls.
- batchSize must be >= 1, otherwise error out before doing anything.
- Don't trust the inputs: a key <= its predecessor within a sequence means the dump is broken. Equal consecutive keys -> ErrDuplicateKey; decreasing -> ErrUnsorted. Because this must stay single-pass over huge dumps, validate AS you walk: full batches emitted before the bad element are already flushed and stay flushed, the in-progress partial batch is dropped, and the error comes back.
